topic: What may and may not be sent; ID; third party; repeaters (T1D, T1F)

notes.front: How does Part 97 define broadcasting?
notes.back: Transmissions intended for reception by the general public, either direct or relayed.
notes.explanation: Amateur stations must not engage in any form of broadcasting (97.113(b)); the amateur bands are for communication between amateurs.
notes.example: A commercial FM station’s programme, aimed at anyone who tunes in, is broadcasting; a message to other amateurs is not.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are third-party communications?
notes.back: A message from the control operator (first party) to another station’s control operator (second party) on behalf of another person (third party).
notes.explanation: They let unlicensed people send messages by amateur radio, but only under the rules in 97.115.
notes.example: Your unlicensed neighbour asks you to pass a message to an amateur (ham) in another state: you are the first party, the amateur the second, your neighbour the third.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is model craft control in amateur radio?
notes.back: Using an amateur station to send control signals to a model craft, such as a model aircraft, boat or car.
notes.explanation: Part 97 gives these transmissions special treatment on identification, codes and power (97.215).
notes.example: Flying a model aeroplane with a transmitter on an amateur frequency.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is a tactical call sign?
notes.back: A name such as “Race Headquarters” used on the air; it never replaces your FCC-assigned call sign.
notes.explanation: Tactical calls are handy in events and emergencies, but the identification rules still require your own call sign.
notes.example: At a marathon, the station at the finish line calls itself “Finish Line” and still gives its call sign every 10 minutes.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is a self-assigned indicator?
notes.back: Words, letters or numerals you choose to add before or after your call sign during identification, separated from it.
notes.explanation: It must be separated from the call sign, and must not conflict with an indicator the FCC rules specify or with another country’s prefix (97.119(c)).
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.3(a)(25) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T1F06
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: With which countries may FCC-licensed amateur stations not exchange messages?
notes.back: Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications.
notes.explanation: The objection is made to the ITU, not to any amateur organisation (97.111(a)(1)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: May an amateur station engage in broadcasting?
notes.back: No: an amateur station must not engage in any form of broadcasting.
notes.explanation: One-way transmissions are also banned unless the rules specifically allow them (97.113(b)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Are brief adjustment transmissions, Morse code practice and telemetry allowed as one-way transmissions?
notes.back: Yes: all three are one-way transmissions 97.111(b) allows.
notes.explanation: The full list also includes brief calls to set up two-way contact, telecommand, emergency communications and information bulletins.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may an amateur station send messages encoded to obscure their meaning?
notes.back: Only when sending control commands to space stations or model craft.
notes.explanation: Obscuring codes are otherwise banned (97.113(a)(4)); telecommand stations may encode commands to a space station (97.211(b)), and model craft control signals are not treated as codes (97.215(b)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may an amateur station transmit music using a phone emission?
notes.back: Only when incidental to an authorised retransmission of manned spacecraft communications.
notes.explanation: Music is otherwise banned (97.113(a)(4)); 97.113(c) allows retransmitting manned spacecraft communications, including incidental music, with NASA’s prior approval.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may you tell other amateurs about equipment for sale or trade?
notes.back: When it is apparatus normally used in an amateur station and you do not do it on a regular basis.
notes.explanation: It is an exception to the ban on communications in which you have a financial interest (97.113(a)(3)(ii)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Is any obscene or indecent language allowed on amateur frequencies?
notes.back: No: obscene or indecent words or language are prohibited.
notes.explanation: The prohibition covers any such language (97.113(a)(4)); the pool rejects the idea of an FCC or ITU word list.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.113(a)(4) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T1D06
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Under which exception may a teacher be paid while acting as control operator?
notes.back: When the station is used as part of classroom instruction at an educational institution.
notes.explanation: Communications for hire are otherwise prohibited (97.113(a)(2)); the teaching exception is 97.113(a)(3)(iii).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may amateur stations send information to broadcasters for news gathering?
notes.back: Only for communications directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when no other means is reasonably available.
notes.explanation: 97.113(b) otherwise bars amateur stations from programme production and news gathering for broadcasting.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may a station controlling a model craft skip on-air identification?
notes.back: When a label showing the call sign and the licensee’s name and address is fixed to the transmitter.
notes.explanation: This applies only to transmissions directed at the model craft (97.215(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: A transmitter used to control a model craft may put out no more than {{c1::1 W}} of power.
notes.explanation: Model control gets its own rule, 97.215: no on-air identification if the transmitter carries a label with the call sign and the licensee’s name and address, and a power cap of 1 W.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Must on-the-air test transmissions be identified?
notes.back: Yes: identify the transmitting station, as for any other transmission.
notes.explanation: No station may transmit unidentified communications or signals (97.119(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: You must send your call sign at the end of each communication and at least every {{c1::10 minutes}} during it.
notes.explanation: The rule is 97.119(a); there is no requirement to identify at the start of a contact.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When you use a tactical call sign, how often must you still give your FCC-assigned call sign?
notes.back: At least every 10 minutes during, and at the end of, the communication.
notes.explanation: A tactical call sign never replaces the identification rule in 97.119(a).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: In what language must you identify when using a phone emission?
notes.back: English.
notes.explanation: 97.119(b)(2) requires phone identification in the English language; using a phonetic alphabet is encouraged.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: A station is transmitting phone. By which emissions may it send its call sign?
notes.back: By CW or by phone.
notes.explanation: The call sign must be sent with an emission authorised on the channel; 97.119(b) lists CW and phone (in English) among the ways.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: How must a self-assigned indicator be separated from the call sign?
notes.back: By the slant mark (/) or any suitable word that denotes it, such as “stroke”, “slant” or “slash”.
notes.explanation: 97.119(c) allows the indicator before, after, or both before and after the call sign.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.119(c) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T1F06
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: An automatic device that sends a station’s CW identification must not go faster than {{c1::20}} words per minute.
notes.explanation: The limit is in 97.119(b)(1).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When may you pass a third party’s message to a station in a foreign country?
notes.back: When that country has an arrangement with the US for third-party traffic, or for emergency or disaster relief communications.
notes.explanation: Without such an arrangement it is banned, unless the third party is eligible to be a control operator of the station (97.115(a)(2)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: A repeater accidentally retransmits a message that breaks the rules. Is the repeater’s control operator accountable?
notes.back: No. The repeater’s control operator is not accountable; the originating station’s control operator is.
notes.explanation: 97.205(g) exempts the repeater’s control operator for inadvertent retransmissions; the pool holds the originating station’s control operator accountable.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.205(g) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T1F10
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When must the station licensee make the station and its records available for inspection?
notes.back: At any time, upon request by an FCC representative.
notes.explanation: No written notice, waiting period or warrant is required by the rule (97.103(c)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: With which countries are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations prohibited from exchanging communications?
notes.back: Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications
notes.choices:
A) Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications
B) Any country whose administration has notified the American Radio Relay League (ARRL) that it objects to such communications
C) Any country banned from such communications by the International Amateur Radio Union (IARU)
D) Any country banned from making such communications by the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
notes.choicesExplained: B: the ARRL is an amateur organisation; objections go to the ITU. C: the IARU does not ban countries; the ITU notification is what counts. D: the ARRL cannot ban countries.
notes.explanation: Stations may not exchange messages with any country whose administration has told the ITU it objects (97.111(a)(1)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Under which of the following circumstances are one-way transmissions by an amateur station prohibited?
notes.back: Broadcasting
notes.choices:
A) Announcements of upcoming ham radio operating events
B) Broadcasting
C) International Morse Code Practice
D) Telecommand or transmissions of telemetry
notes.choicesExplained: A: announcements of events for amateurs are information bulletins, which 97.111(b)(6) allows. C: Morse code practice is allowed by 97.111(b)(5). D: telecommand and telemetry are allowed by 97.111(b)(3) and (7).
notes.explanation: Broadcasting is prohibited (97.113(b)); announcements, Morse practice, telecommand and telemetry are among the permitted one-way transmissions (97.111(b)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When is it permissible to transmit messages encoded to obscure their meaning?
notes.back: Only when transmitting control commands to space stations or model craft
notes.choices:
A) Only when using a remote station during a contest
B) Only when transmitting certain approved digital codes
C) Only when transmitting control commands to space stations or model craft
D) Never
notes.choicesExplained: A: contests and remote stations are not exceptions. B: no digital code is approved for obscuring meaning. D: there are two exceptions, so “never” is wrong.
notes.explanation: Obscuring codes are banned except for control commands to space stations (97.211(b)) and model craft, whose control signals are not treated as codes (97.215(b); 97.113(a)(4)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Under what conditions is an amateur station authorized to transmit music using a phone emission?
notes.back: When incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications
notes.choices:
A) When incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications
B) When the music produces no spurious emissions
C) When transmissions are limited to less than three minutes per hour
D) When the music is transmitted above 1280 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: spurious emissions have nothing to do with the music ban. C: there is no three-minutes-per-hour allowance. D: the ban applies on every frequency.
notes.explanation: Music is banned except when incidental to an authorised retransmission of manned spacecraft communications (97.113(a)(4), 97.113(c)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When may amateur radio operators use their stations to notify other amateurs of the availability of equipment for sale or trade?
notes.back: When selling amateur radio equipment and not on a regular basis
notes.choices:
A) Never
B) When the equipment is not the personal property of either the station licensee, or the control operator, or their close relatives
C) When no profit is made on the sale
D) When selling amateur radio equipment and not on a regular basis
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rules do allow occasional sale notices. B: the rule does not depend on who owns the equipment. C: the test is regularity, not whether a profit is made.
notes.explanation: You may advertise amateur equipment for sale or trade, provided you do not do it on a regular basis (97.113(a)(3)(ii)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What, if any, are the restrictions concerning transmission of language that may be considered indecent or obscene?
notes.back: Any such language is prohibited
notes.choices:
A) The FCC maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
B) Any such language is prohibited
C) The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
D) There is no such prohibition
notes.choicesExplained: A: the FCC keeps no list of banned words; all such language is banned. C: the ITU keeps no such list either. D: there is a prohibition, in 97.113(a)(4).
notes.explanation: The rule bans “obscene or indecent words or language” outright (97.113(a)(4)). It does not rely on any list, so no FCC or ITU list decides what is allowed.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following is an example of an auxiliary station?
notes.back: A station sending one-way transmissions between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter
notes.choices:
A) A station sending one-way transmissions between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter
B) A backup radio for emergency use in case the main station radio fails
C) A station used in the Military Auxiliary Radio System for linking government and amateur stations in a digital network
D) A second station utilized in multi-operator contest stations
notes.choicesExplained: B: a backup radio is just spare equipment for the same station. C: the Military Auxiliary Radio System links to government stations; an auxiliary station links amateur stations within an amateur system (97.3(a)(7)). D: a second contest station is simply another station, not a link within a system.
notes.explanation: A link between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter is point-to-point within a system of cooperating stations (97.3(a)(7)); auxiliary stations may send one-way communications (97.201(e)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: In which of the following circumstances may the control operator of an amateur station receive compensation for operating that station?
notes.back: When the communication is a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution
notes.choices:
A) When the communication is related to the sale of amateur equipment by the control operator's employer
B) When the communication is a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution
C) When the communication is made to obtain emergency information for a local broadcast station
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: communications on behalf of an employer’s sales are a banned financial interest. C: gathering information for a broadcast station is not a paid exception. D: only B is correct.
notes.explanation: A control operator may be paid as part of a teaching job when the station is used in classroom instruction at an educational institution (97.113(a)(3)(iii)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When may amateur stations transmit information in support of broadcasting, program production, or news gathering, assuming no other means is available?
notes.back: When such communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
notes.choices:
A) When such communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
B) When broadcasting communications to or from the space shuttle
C) Where non-commercial programming is gathered and supplied exclusively to the National Public Radio network
D) Never
notes.choicesExplained: B: there is no space shuttle exception for broadcasting. C: non-commercial programming is not an exception. D: the safety-of-life exception exists, so “never” is wrong.
notes.explanation: Only communications directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property may be given to broadcasters (97.113(b); the pool prints this as “97.113(5)(b)”).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: How does the FCC define broadcasting for the Amateur Radio Service?
notes.back: Transmissions intended for reception by the general public
notes.choices:
A) Two-way transmissions by amateur stations
B) Any transmission made by the licensed station
C) Transmission of messages directed only to amateur operators
D) Transmissions intended for reception by the general public
notes.choicesExplained: A: two-way contacts are normal amateur communication. B: most transmissions by a licensed station are not broadcasting. C: messages directed only to amateurs are information bulletins, which are allowed.
notes.explanation: The key words are “intended for reception by the general public” (97.3(a)(10)). Amateur messages are aimed at other amateurs, which is why broadcasting is banned (97.113(b)) but bulletins for amateurs are not.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When may an amateur station transmit without identifying on the air?
notes.back: When transmitting signals to control model craft
notes.choices:
A) When the transmissions are of a brief nature to make station adjustments
B) When the transmissions are unmodulated
C) When the transmitted power level is below 0.1 watt
D) When transmitting signals to control model craft
notes.choicesExplained: A: brief adjustment transmissions must still be identified. B: unmodulated signals must still be identified. C: there is no low-power exemption from identification.
notes.explanation: Transmissions directed only to a model craft need no on-air identification if a label with the call sign and licensee’s name and address is on the transmitter (97.215(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following is required when making on-the-air test transmissions?
notes.back: Identify the transmitting station
notes.choices:
A) Identify the transmitting station
B) Conduct tests only between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. local time
C) Notify the FCC of the transmissions
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: there are no set hours for tests. C: no FCC notice is needed. D: only A is correct.
notes.explanation: Test transmissions must be identified like any other; no station may send unidentified signals (97.119(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When must the station licensee make the station and the station records available for inspection?
notes.back: At any time upon request by an FCC representative
notes.choices:
A) At any time ten days after notification by the FCC of such an inspection
B) At any time upon request by an FCC representative
C) At any time after a written notification by the FCC of such inspection
D) Only when presented with a valid warrant by an FCC official or government agent
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no ten-day wait. C: no written notice is required. D: no warrant is required.
notes.explanation: The licensee is responsible for the proper operation of the station (97.103(a)), and the rule makes the station and records available upon request by an FCC representative (97.103(c)), with no waiting period, notice or warrant in it.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: How often must you identify with your FCC-assigned call sign when using tactical call signs such as “Race Headquarters”?
notes.back: At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
notes.choices:
A) Never, the tactical call is sufficient
B) Once every hour
C) At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
D) At the end of every transmission
notes.choicesExplained: A: the tactical call alone does not identify your station. B: once an hour is too seldom. D: identifying after every transmission is not what the rule requires.
notes.explanation: A tactical call sign does not replace your own: identify at least every 10 minutes and at the end (97.119(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When are you required to transmit your assigned call sign?
notes.back: At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
notes.choices:
A) At the beginning of each contact, and every 10 minutes thereafter
B) At least once during each transmission
C) At least every 15 minutes during and at the end of a communication
D) At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no requirement to identify at the beginning. B: the rule is time-based, not per transmission. C: the interval is 10 minutes, not 15.
notes.explanation: Identification exists to make the source of the transmissions clearly known to those receiving (97.119(a)); a fixed 10-minute interval, plus once at the end, does that without a call sign before every transmission.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What language must you use for identification when using a phone emission?
notes.back: English
notes.choices:
A) Any language recognized by the United Nations
B) Any language recognized by the ITU
C) English
D) English, French, or Spanish
notes.choicesExplained: A: being recognized by the UN does not make a language acceptable; phone identification must be in English. B: ITU recognition is irrelevant; English is required. D: French and Spanish are not allowed for phone identification.
notes.explanation: Identification exists so that those receiving can tell which station is transmitting (97.119(a)), and the rule requires phone identification “in the English language” (97.119(b)(2)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What method of call sign identification is required for a station transmitting phone signals?
notes.back: Send the call sign using a CW or phone emission
notes.choices:
A) Send the call sign followed by the indicator RPT
B) Send the call sign using a CW or phone emission
C) Send the call sign followed by the indicator R
D) Send the call sign using only a phone emission
notes.choicesExplained: A: no RPT indicator is required. C: no R indicator is required. D: CW is also allowed, so “only phone” is wrong.
notes.explanation: The call sign must be sent with an emission authorized for the channel, and both CW and phone in English are listed ways of sending it (97.119(b)(1), (2)); no RPT or R indicator is part of the rule.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following self-assigned indicators are acceptable when using a phone transmission?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) KL7CC stroke W3
B) KL7CC slant W3
C) KL7CC slash W3
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: “stroke” is acceptable, but so are the others. B: “slant” is acceptable, but so are the others. C: “slash” is acceptable, but so are the others.
notes.explanation: An indicator may be separated by the slant mark or any suitable word denoting it, so “stroke”, “slant” and “slash” all qualify (97.119(c)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following restrictions apply when a non-licensed person speaks to a foreign amateur radio station via a station under the control of an FCC-licensed amateur radio operator?
notes.back: The foreign station must be in a country with which the U.S. has a third-party agreement
notes.choices:
A) The person must be a U.S. citizen
B) The foreign station must be in a country with which the U.S. has a third-party agreement
C) The licensed control operator must do the station identification
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: the third party need not be a US citizen. C: no rule requires the control operator personally to say the call sign; 97.119 requires the station to identify. D: only B is a restriction that applies (97.115(a)(2)).
notes.explanation: Third-party messages to a foreign station need an arrangement between that country and the US (97.115(a)(2)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is the definition of third-party communications?
notes.back: A message from a control operator to another amateur station control operator on behalf of another person
notes.choices:
A) A message from a control operator to another amateur station control operator on behalf of another person
B) Amateur radio communications where three stations are in communications with one another
C) Operation when the transmitting equipment is licensed to a person other than the control operator
D) Temporary authorization for an unlicensed person to transmit on the amateur bands for technical experiments
notes.choicesExplained: B: three stations talking together is simply a group contact. C: operating someone else’s station, once designated, makes you its control operator, not a third party. D: there is no temporary authorisation for unlicensed people to transmit.
notes.explanation: The definition counts parties: the control operator is the first party, the other station’s control operator the second, and the person on whose behalf the message is sent the third (97.3(a)(47)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What type of amateur station simultaneously retransmits the signal of another amateur station on a different channel or channels?
notes.back: Repeater station
notes.choices:
A) Beacon station
B) Remote control station
C) Repeater station
D) Message forwarding station
notes.choicesExplained: A: a beacon transmits for observing propagation and reception (97.3(a)(9)); it does not retransmit others. B: remote control is a way of controlling a station, not a type of retransmitting station. D: a message forwarding system passes messages from an originating to a destination control operator (97.3(a)(32)); the definition asked is the repeater’s.
notes.explanation: Only auxiliary, repeater and space stations may automatically retransmit other amateurs’ signals (97.113(d)); the one defined by simultaneous retransmission on a different channel is the repeater (97.3(a)(40)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Who is accountable if a repeater inadvertently retransmits communications that violate the FCC rules?
notes.back: The control operator of the originating station
notes.choices:
A) The control operator of the originating station
B) The control operator of the repeater
C) The owner of the repeater
D) Both the originating station and the repeater owner
notes.choicesExplained: B: 97.205(g) exempts the repeater’s control operator. C: the owner did not originate the communication. D: only the originating station is accountable.
notes.explanation: The repeater’s control operator is not accountable for inadvertent retransmissions (97.205(g)); the originating station’s control operator is.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: How does a repeater differ from an auxiliary station?
notes.back: A repeater simultaneously retransmits other stations on a different channel; an auxiliary station links cooperating stations point-to-point.
notes.explanation: An auxiliary station is often part of a repeater system, e.g. linking a remote receiver to the main transmitter (97.3(a)(7), (40)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Both are one-way. Why are information bulletins allowed but broadcasting is not?
notes.back: Information bulletins are directed only to amateur operators; broadcasting is intended for the general public.
notes.explanation: Information bulletins carry only subject matter of direct interest to the amateur service (97.3(a)(26)) and are allowed by 97.111(b)(6).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Your unlicensed friend speaks through your station to another US amateur while you supervise at the control point. What kind of communication is this?
notes.back: Third-party communications.
notes.explanation: You are the first party, the other control operator the second, your friend the third; a third party may speak if the control operator supervises continuously (97.115(b)(1)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)
